units.name: Ch1-1 History of Money
units.passage: Today, people pay for things with coins and paper bills. Long before these existed, however, people traded with many kinds of materials, and they usually chose things that had great value. Salt is one of the oldest examples of money. In ancient Rome, soldiers and officers received salt as payment, so the Latin word "salarium" came to mean the pay of a soldier. The English word "salary," which means the money a worker gets from an employer every month, grew out of this Latin word. Much later, salt was so precious in many areas of Africa that people traded with bars of it. Even now, nomads in Tibet use cakes of salt in the same way as coins. Metal also played a role. Over 4,000 years ago, people in China used tiny copies of fine metal tools, and these small objects later developed into the first coins of the modern kind. One of the most interesting stories comes from Colonial America. Back then, Native Americans highly valued deer skins and horns. Early white settlers sold these goods to them and counted the skins as "bucks," a word for deer skin. That is why Americans still call dollars "bucks" in casual speech today.

units.name: Ch1-2 London's Taxi Drivers
units.passage: Finding your way through the streets of London is not easy, because they are very complicated. Still, the city's taxi drivers are well known for knowing every road and place. For more than 150 years, anyone who wants to become a cab driver in London has had to pass a test called the "Knowledge." This test is very hard, and people usually study the roads for three years or more before they pass. Because of this training, a London driver understands at once where a passenger wants to go. Imagine you say, "I'd like to go to that restaurant on Hereford Road named after a woman." The driver would answer right away: "Veronica's." Students take classes, but after class they (a) go out onto the streets. In this way, they connect what they learned in the classroom with the real city, because seeing something with your own eyes is the best way to learn. Little by little, they learn the whole map of London. These days, however, the drivers face a new problem. Rideshare cars with GPS offer trips for half the price. Even so, London's cab drivers believe their knowledge of the city puts them ahead, since they can take passengers where they want to go faster and more efficiently.

units.name: Ch1-3 Urban Legends
units.passage: An urban legend is a kind of folktale for modern times. It is a made-up story that people pass on by talking to each other. Some of these stories sound so real that lots of people accept them as facts. Strangely, though, the events always seem to involve a friend of a friend whom nobody has met, and no one can find out where the story began. It usually has many versions, and it often carries a warning or a lesson. One such story has made many New Yorkers lose sleep. It says that huge alligators are hiding under the streets of New York City. In the story, a local family took a trip to Florida and came home with a baby alligator. When the animal grew too large and became too much trouble, the family got rid of it by flushing it down the toilet. Somehow the alligator stayed alive, and many years afterward it (a) started to attack sewer workers and other people. People have repeated this story for decades. In reality, however, alligators cannot survive in sewers because of the cold and the bacteria. In 1982, the city's sewer bureau even announced this officially. Still, some people refuse to accept it and keep believing the monster is real. What lesson do you think this legend teaches?

units.name: Ch1-4 Foods Born from War
units.passage: Napoleon is said to have believed that an army travels on its stomach. He understood that soldiers need good food in order to fight well. Hungry soldiers cannot win a battle, but a battlefield is also no place for a long, fancy dinner. So during wars, people created meals that were fast and simple to make but still filling. Surprisingly, several foods we love today started as these war meals. Take kebab, for example. In Turkish, the word means "meat grilled on a stick." Ottoman soldiers grilled meat on their swords over fires in open fields. Cutting the meat into small pieces made it cook faster and used less firewood, which was hard to find in the desert. Shabu-shabu also has a war story. It began on Mongolian battlefields in the 1200s, when Genghis Khan boiled thin slices of meat in his war helmet and fed his soldiers. Like kebab, the thin meat cooked quickly and saved fuel. Hotteok, a snack Koreans also love, first came from China. It was made during war to replace steamed dumplings. Because it was baked instead of steamed, it was simple to cook and keep. These foods, made to survive in a hurry, spread to ordinary people around the world. Isn't it strange that such wonderful dishes came from terrible wars?

items.exp: 칭기즈칸은 투구를 냄비로 써서 얇게 썬 고기를 삶았다(boiled thin slices of meat)고 했어요.

units.name: Ch1-5 China's Regional Gap
units.passage: China has a serious problem: some of its regions are much richer than others. The communist government tried to make this gap smaller by giving special benefits to people from poor areas. These efforts did not fully work, so the government started market reforms. Sadly, the gap between regions has grown even wider since then. Poor provinces have been left behind, while rich ones have become even richer. Since the reforms began, most of the gains have gone to Beijing, the capital, and to the coastal region. Guangdong and Fujian, two provinces in the south, have gained the most. This coastal area has been known for trading with other countries for a long time, and its location has been a great advantage. The two provinces have strong ties with overseas Chinese communities in Southeast Asia and North America. They (a) are also near Taiwan and Hong Kong. Through these two routes, huge amounts of money have poured into the southern coast from Chinese business networks. In addition, companies from America, Japan, and Europe have made large investments in the area. As a result, the south coast has grown fast, while many inland areas still struggle.

units.name: Ch1-6 History of Shoes
units.passage: When did people first start wearing shoes? Experts guess that about 40,000 years ago, humans probably made some type of footwear to keep their feet safe from the cold. The oldest real footwear ever found, however, is a pair of sandals from California, made around 9,000 years ago. As for Europe, the earliest shoes there were moccasin-like coverings made from the skins of deer and bears. In other words, the first shoes were made in different ways depending on what people needed. Today we choose shoes not only to protect our feet but also to show our style and wealth. Yet it took humans a long time to be able to buy whatever shoes they wanted. Shoes are part of a bigger history, so their styles in each period were shaped by social, economic, and political conditions as well as by climate. For example, shoes in ancient Rome showed a person's social class. Soldiers, nobles, and ordinary people all wore sandals, but each group wore a different kind. Similarly, in the Middle Ages, when people could not change their class, shoes showed how high a person's rank was. Later, the walls between classes slowly broke down, and wealth became a more important measure. Finally, in modern times, money rather than class decides which shoes people buy and wear.

units.name: Ch1-7 Different Views of Time
units.passage: In American culture, people think it is important to be on time and to follow the schedule they first planned. In some other cultures, however, these ideas may not matter much, because people there think about time in a less fixed way. Some cultures are called monochronic. People in these cultures like to finish one task before they move on to the next one. In contrast, people in polychronic societies try to handle several tasks at once. In such cultures, doing many things together is valued, but people never let it push aside their relationships with others. Being polite and kind is more important to them than meeting deadlines. This difference helps explain why Americans often find it hard to work with people from polychronic cultures. Because most Americans are monochronic, they (a) may think certain polychronic behaviors are rude. For instance, a person might stop a face-to-face talk to answer a phone call. However, that person does not mean to be rude at all. People from polychronic cultures simply deal with the tasks in front of them in a different way, and they expect others to understand this.

units.name: Ch1-8 Reading Emotions
units.passage: Humans are social creatures, and we show and share our feelings with other people. For a long time, scientists have wanted to know how we figure out what others are feeling. Most studies on this question have looked at words and facial expressions. A group of scientists in Japan, however, carried out a new experiment and discovered something interesting. They filmed actors saying the phrase "Is that so?", which has no special emotional meaning. The actors said it in two ways: with an angry tone of voice and a happy face, and with a happy tone of voice and an angry face. The videos were made in both Japanese and Dutch. Next, volunteers from Japan and the Netherlands watched the videos and had to decide whether each speaker was happy or angry. The results showed that the Japanese volunteers focused more on the tone of voice than the Dutch volunteers did. On the other hand, the Dutch volunteers paid closer attention to facial expressions. The study tells us two important things. First, tone of voice is another key factor, along with words and faces, in understanding how others feel. Second, people from different cultures give different amounts of weight to these three factors.

units.name: Ch2-1 Life on a Submarine
units.passage: Living aboard a submarine is far from easy, and the biggest challenge is a lack of room. Many sailors share a very small area, so every corner matters. A submarine is a warship, so it has to hold weapons, computers, and lots of other machines. On top of that, the crew needs somewhere to live. To deal with this problem, sailors have found a smart way to make the most of every bit of room: one area is used for several purposes at once. The living area works as a place to sleep, eat, and relax. At night, each sailor sleeps in a capsule that is smaller than a closet, so there is no room to turn over in bed. Personal items go into very small lockers, and clothes are stored under thin mattresses. This idea is called the "double-duty" rule. For instance, the dining area also becomes a movie theater, and the restroom doubles as a place to keep food. Because life underwater is so hard and stressful, psychologists check the sailors regularly. They make sure no one suffers from anxiety problems like claustrophobia, which is the fear of small, closed places.

units.name: Ch2-2 The Window Tax
units.passage: In 1696, England began charging a tax on windows. Back then, glass cost a lot, so it was a sign of being rich. Large houses had many windows, which showed that the people living in them had enough money to pay higher taxes. Homes with more than six windows had to pay. A house with seven to nine windows was charged two shillings, while a house with ten to nineteen windows was charged four shillings. Over time, the government kept making the tax higher. It was simple to collect, because anyone could count the windows from the street. To escape the tax, some owners covered their windows with boards. Before long, houses with fewer windows became the fashion, and some people even lived in homes with no windows at all. However, as cities filled with people, this led to trouble. Homes without light were dark and wet, and people living in them got sick. Critics gave it nicknames such as "tax on health" and "tax on light and air." People also thought it was unfair, since it put a heavy load on middle- and lower-class families. In 1851, this hated tax was finally replaced with a tax on houses. Still, even today it is easy to find old buildings without windows in England.

units.name: Ch2-3 Good Samaritan Laws
units.passage: Have you ever met someone who needed help from a doctor? Imagine that a person near you suddenly has a heart attack. You must begin CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) immediately, before it is too late. However, there is a problem: you might hurt the person while helping, and this could get you into trouble. Even though you meant well, you could be taken to court for the injury. The person or his family may not realize that you were only trying to help. So, what should you do? Don't hold back. Many countries, including Korea, Japan, France, Germany, and the United States, have Good Samaritan laws. These laws protect people who help others in an emergency. The name comes from a story in the Bible about a Samaritan who helped a man in deep trouble without asking for anything in return. Under these laws, a person who chooses to help cannot be sued. As a result, people can help someone in danger without worrying about legal problems.

units.name: Ch2-4 From La Boheme to Rent
units.passage: Puccini's La Boheme is a great work of art, and fans of classical music see it as one of the finest operas ever written. People often suggest it as the best choice for someone watching an opera for the first time. Still, many people, especially young people, think operas are very dull. Not long ago, one artist found a way to help today's young audiences enjoy this classic story. Jonathan Larson, a composer, wrote Rent, a rock musical that is based on La Boheme. Some parts of the plot have changed, but the main story and the characters of Rent follow those of the opera. The characters in the two works have names that are alike or even the same, and they also do similar jobs. However, some things were changed to match modern times. In La Boheme, a character named Mimi has tuberculosis, but in Rent, she has AIDS. The opera is set in Paris in the 1830s, while the musical is set in New York in the 1990s. The two shows use very different kinds of music, but their message is the same: it is still hard to live as an artist and find true love in a large city.

units.name: Ch2-5 Redefining the Kilogram
units.passage: In many fields of science, measuring things exactly is very important. But how can we be sure that a measurement is exact? To answer this, we need absolute standards, and countries around the world have agreed on them. For example, after the Treaty of the Metre was signed in 1875, the kilogram came to be defined by a single piece of metal called "Le Grand K," kept in a locked vault in France. The problem is that solid objects slowly change over time. When scientists weighed Le Grand K in the 1980s, it had lost a few micrograms, so every scientific scale had to be recalibrated. Scientists realized they needed a universal constant, a value that stays the same today and millions of years from now. So, they redefined the units using constants of nature. A second is no longer one 86,400th of a day; it is now 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a particular microwave beam. A meter is no longer the length of a metal bar made in 1889; it is how far light moves in a vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second. The kilogram problem was also solved by physics: it is now defined using the Planck constant, h. This may sound hard to understand, but it is a giant step forward for science.

items.q: 글의 요지로 가장 알맞은 것은?
choices: 물체는 시간이 지나며 변하므로, 변하지 않는 상수로 측정 단위를 새로 정의했다.
킬로그램의 기준은 앞으로도 금속 덩어리로 유지되어야 한다.
과학 연구에서 정확한 측정은 별로 중요하지 않다.
items.exp: 고체 물체인 Le Grand K의 무게가 변한 문제를, 영원히 변하지 않는 자연의 상수로 단위를 재정의하여 해결했다는 내용이에요.

items.q: 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

1초는 이제 특별한 마이크로파의 진동 수로 정의된다.
미터의 옛 기준은 1889년에 만든 금속 막대였다.
Le Grand K는 1980년대에 무게가 더 무거워졌다.
items.exp: 1980년대에 무게를 쟀을 때 몇 마이크로그램 가벼워졌다(had lost a few micrograms)고 했어요.

choices: a number or value that never changes

items.exp: constant는 '항상 일정한 값을 가진 수나 양'이라는 뜻이에요.

items.exp: A meter is ... how far light moves in a vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second라고 했어요. 금속 막대는 옛 기준이고, 플랑크 상수는 킬로그램에 쓰여요.

units.name: Ch2-6 Watching Workers at Home
units.passage: Do you believe that your activity on your office computer is private? You may want to think again, because your boss could be watching you closely. Watching workers is not a new idea, but as more people work from home, companies now use special software that follows workers even into their homes. This software can record every key you press and every website you visit. It does more than watch, though. It also analyzes, ranks, and reports on how productive each worker is. All of this is legal as long as companies tell workers about it. It is true that being watched makes people behave a little better. However, it also makes them feel uneasy, and they become afraid to try new things or be creative. So, for the system to work well, surveillance has to be transparent. First, the employer should clearly explain what is being measured. Second, the employer should decide on a clear purpose for watching and focus only on that issue, instead of checking every part of a worker's behavior. In the future, more people will work from home with flexible hours, and watching workers will quickly become normal. This change gives us a chance to look again at how surveillance is done so that both workers and employers can benefit.

units.name: Ch2-7 Bringing Back Extinct Animals
units.passage: We humans often forget how important biodiversity is to our lives. We do not see that we are a deep part of it, and that if we harm nature, the damage will come back to us. Old ways of protecting nature have not been fast enough to keep up with how quickly it is being destroyed. Now, however, a new helper has appeared. Biotechnology has recently made great progress in reviving extinct species, a process called "de-extinction." This technology is complicated, and people argue about it. Basically, it brings animals that have died out, or animals very close to them, back to life. These revived animals could be released back into nature and play the important roles in nature that they (a) played before they disappeared. Take the woolly mammoth, for instance. This animal, which died out 4,000 years ago, might return. Scientists could use genetic engineering to change the genes of the Asian elephant, the mammoth's closest living relative. Still, many questions remain because we know so little about these species. In other words, technology is moving faster than our understanding of the species and how they would fit in the real world. What is frightening is that once we interfere with something as basic as recreating species, we cannot go back.

units.name: Ch2-8 Can GM Crops End Hunger
units.passage: Hunger remains one of the biggest problems facing the world in the twenty-first century. Although things have gotten somewhat better, over 800 million people worldwide still do not get enough nutrition. Scientists are searching for ways to deal with this problem, and one idea is to use genetically modified (GM) crops. But can they really work? GM crops are plants whose DNA has been changed through genetic engineering to give them useful traits. This technology can help farmers grow more food. It can also help plants fight off pests better. In addition, crops can be made more nutritious so that they provide important nutrients to people who need them. However, several problems must be solved before GM crops can truly fight hunger. First, many people worry that GM foods are not safe, even though there is no solid evidence for these worries. Second, only a few large companies, which own the rights to the genetic changes, make most GM seeds. If one of these companies went out of business, its crops would no longer be available, which is an economic risk to food security. Third, farmers in areas suffering from hunger lack education and information, so GM crops spread too slowly there to make a real difference.

items.q: 글의 요지로 가장 알맞은 것은?

units.name: Ch3-1 The Good Side of Boredom
units.passage: Have you ever felt so bored that you thought you might die of it? People often tell us that wasting time is harmful and that we must stay busy every minute. Many also believe that the brain simply shuts down when there is nothing to do. Research, however, suggests the opposite: boredom can actually draw out our creative side. Of course, boredom is not a pleasant feeling. It is dull, and it makes us feel restless and unchallenged. Yet this uncomfortable feeling also works as a push. Remember how many ideas pop into your head while you are doing nothing at all. In fact, our brains come up with creative thoughts precisely because we are bored. When bored people notice that their present situation has no excitement, they (a) become more eager to try meaningful or interesting activities. They drive themselves to search for something fresh. So, next time you feel bored, do not rush to fill the empty time. Just let your mind wander freely. You may be about to discover some interesting new ideas.

items.exp: 통념(지루함은 나쁘고 뇌가 멈춘다)을 소개한 뒤, 지루함이 오히려 창의성을 끌어낸다고 반박하는 글이에요.

units.name: Ch3-2 Cell Phones in Class Discussion
units.passage: These days, cell phones are creating a lot of problems in schools. Students want to use their phones during the school day, but most teachers do not permit this, and some even collect the phones before class starts. A small number of teachers in the US, however, are taking a different approach. They use social media on cell phones as a tool to get students talking in class. Before this change, only around 30% of the students in their classes joined in discussions. After the students were allowed to share ideas through their phones, over 70% of them participated. It seems that many students felt more at ease typing their thoughts on a phone screen than speaking up in front of everyone. Even so, most teachers still have doubts about bringing social media into the classroom. They are afraid that students will lose focus on their schoolwork. They also worry that students might post rude or improper comments. To sum up, using social media for class discussion is certainly a fresh and creative idea. However, we need more time to decide how it can be used in the right way.

units.name: Ch3-3 Why Women's Soccer Is More Fun
units.passage: Do you enjoy watching soccer? A lot of fans believe that men's soccer is just more fun to watch than women's soccer. It is true that male players are more athletic. They run faster and kick the ball with more power. However, I would argue that women's soccer can be more interesting if you look at the game in a different way. First of all, women's games are more attack-focused. Female players are usually smaller than male players, so each player has to cover a larger part of the field. As a result, more open spaces appear, and players get more chances to shoot. That is why women's matches usually end with more goals. Watching a 5-4 match is far more thrilling than watching a dull 1-1 draw. Second, the women's game is much slower, but that is not a weakness. In fact, it is a strong point. Because the pace is slow, we can enjoy the beautiful teamwork and tactics of the whole team. In the men's game, on the other hand, star players such as Messi and Ronaldo control the match on their own. Women's soccer moves slowly enough for viewers to notice interesting patterns of play, while men's soccer is just too fast.

units.name: Ch3-4 Vocabulary Is the Real Challenge
units.passage: Many people believe that grammar is the hardest part of learning a new language. Learners of German often complain about its famous three genders and four cases. Students of French get very frustrated when they must memorize countless verb forms. It is true that mastering the grammar of a language is not easy. However, I believe that vocabulary is actually the bigger challenge. Understanding grammar requires time and effort, but building vocabulary takes much longer. If you compare learning a single word with understanding one grammar rule, the first (a) seems much simpler than the second. But think about what you need to share your ideas and emotions. You need at least several hundred or even several thousand words. So, reaching a good level of vocabulary surely demands a huge amount of time and effort. This idea also explains the main reason why some languages seem easier or harder to learn than others: it depends on how much vocabulary they share. When two languages have many words that look alike and mean the same thing, learning one from the other becomes much easier. That is why French is much easier for English speakers than Asian languages such as Korean or Japanese.

units.name: Ch3-5 Marketing Means Meeting Needs
units.passage: Many people think marketing simply means selling and advertising, like TV commercials, newspaper ads, or pop-ups on the Internet. However, marketing covers much more than that. At its heart, marketing is about meeting the needs of customers. A lot of sellers make the error of focusing too much on describing their products. They think of their job as selling a product instead of reaching out to the people who buy it. Marketers should try to attract customers, not the experts who judge their products. For example, a company that makes drill bits may believe that its customers want the most efficient drill bit possible. But what customers truly want is a simple and convenient way to make a hole. In other words, people are looking for solutions to the needs of their everyday lives. Many manufacturers are so busy making their products better that they forget the real needs behind them. They forget the reason they created the product in the first place: to solve a customer's problem. The most important thing is to find out which problems customers want to solve in daily life. Therefore, marketing must focus on the needs of customers, not just on the products.

units.name: Ch3-6 Is History Really Objective
units.passage: When people read history books, they usually believe the books show them objective facts about the past. Readers often see these books as neutral records of what happened long ago. As a result, they think that reading history books will give them objective knowledge about earlier times. But is that really true? Do historians believe their job is to write down past events as objectively as they can, without adding their own judgment? Benedetto Croce, a philosopher and historian from Italy, disagreed. He famously said, "All history is contemporary history." What he meant is that history is basically a way of looking at the past through the personal eyes of the present. It may sound odd to call history a subjective work. However, if you think about it carefully, a historian's main task is to judge, not simply to record. If historians did not judge, they could not choose which events are worth recording and which are not. Even though history is subjective, it is still valuable. When you read a history book, you learn not only about the past but also about the present and about the historian who wrote it.

units.name: Ch4-1 The Story of the Pencil
units.passage: Almost everyone uses pencils, and they have existed for nearly 500 years. But when did people begin to use them, and why? The name "pencil" comes from the Latin word penicillum, which means "little tail." In ancient Rome, people wrote letters and documents with these "little tails," small brushes made of different kinds of animal hair. Writing with them was very slow. A writer first had to put the brush into ink, and after writing, he had to let the ink dry fully. If he did not wait, the words would spread and the page would look messy. So how did the modern pencil appear? According to a legend, a violent windstorm started everything. Sometime in the middle of the 1500s, strong winds in England blew down a huge oak tree. Under its roots, people discovered a strange black material. At first, they (a) had no idea how to use it. Then they rubbed it on a sheet of paper, and to their delight, it left a dark line that was already dry. This discovery was the beginning of the pencil we know today. Writers no longer needed to wait for ink to dry.

units.name: Ch4-2 Why We Drive on the Left or Right
units.passage: Why do people in certain countries keep to the right side of the road, while others use the left? Today, about 65% of the world keeps to the right, and the other 35% keeps to the left. Long ago, in feudal times, nearly everyone traveled on the left. This was wise, since violence could break out suddenly. Since 85-90% of people are right-handed, a swordsman stayed on the left so that his right arm was closer to an enemy coming the other way. Later, in 1835, the British government passed a law that ordered riders, coachmen, and everyone else to use the left side. That is why Britain and the countries it once ruled still drive on the left. France and the United States, however, took a different path. In the late 1700s, people there started carrying goods in large wagons. These wagons did not have a seat for the driver, so he (a) usually rode the horse at the back on the left. In this way, his right hand was free to whip the horses. Sitting on the left, he wanted other wagons to pass him on his left side so that their wheels would not hit his. As a result, traffic in these two countries moved to the right, and nations influenced by them did the same.

units.name: Ch4-3 A Blessing in Disguise
units.passage: Americans often say that something is "a blessing in disguise." Do you know what this phrase means? A person can hide his or her face behind a mask, but how can a blessing be hidden? Let's look at a real story that explains it. Max O'Rourke was a 17-year-old football player at a high school in California. He was the star of his team and played quarterback, the most important role on an American football team. Students at his school liked him, and so did the people in his town. Unfortunately, during one game, he broke his leg, and he could not play for the remaining games of the season. After he was hurt and stayed in the hospital, he felt let down and very sad. But then his doctor gave him some shocking news. The X-ray of his leg showed a large tumor that had been growing inside it. Max had surgery, and the doctors removed the tumor successfully. Later, his parents said, "This really was a blessing in disguise. His injury made us so sad, but because of it, the doctors found the tumor, and that discovery saved his life." So a blessing in disguise is something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good.

units.name: Ch4-4 The Ravens of the Tower of London
units.passage: Have you ever wondered why the ravens kept at the Tower of London are unable to fly away? To find the answer, we need to look back at the Tower's history. This Tower is among the best-known buildings in London. William the Conqueror first built it as a fortress. Later, it was also used to store weapons and to hold prisoners. In fact, the Tower is best known for its dark past as a prison and a place of execution. In 1483, the Duke of Gloucester, who later became Richard III, locked up his two nephews there: Prince Edward, aged 12, and Edward's little brother Richard. Nobody ever saw the two boys again. Many famous people were also killed in the Tower, including Sir Thomas More, who wrote Utopia, and Anne Boleyn, the second wife of Henry VIII. During the reign of Charles II, seven "captive ravens" were brought to the Tower so that its bloody history would not happen again. People have long believed that if these birds (a) leave the Tower, the Crown will collapse, and so will Britain. Superstition or not, Britain has not had any violent political unrest since the birds became "captive." This is why the ravens are kept from flying away.

units.name: Ch4-5 The Birth of the Super-Sized Meal
units.passage: Have you ever heard the term "super-sized meal"? This is a way of selling larger burgers, fries, and sodas for just a little more money. McDonald's was the first company to use this term in order to sell more food, and as expected, many customers chose these meals over the regular ones. So where did this sales idea come from? David Wallerstein once worked at a movie theater, where he realized that selling popcorn and Coke was very important for the theater's profit. However, nothing he tried could raise popcorn sales. Then one day he noticed something interesting. Although people wanted more popcorn, no one bought a second box for himself or herself. So Wallerstein made the popcorn boxes larger but charged only slightly more. The result was amazing! People bought more popcorn, and they also drank more Coke. Because of this, the theater's profit grew quickly. Later, when Wallerstein joined McDonald's, he used the same idea to sell fries. He offered larger bags of French fries, and sales went up sharply again. After his success, many other franchises followed this "super-sized" strategy and earned more money. The huge burgers and the many set menus we see today also came from this idea.

units.name: Ch4-6 How Black Friday Got Its Name
units.passage: Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving in the United States, is known around the world for its shopping frenzy. Because this Friday unofficially opened the holiday season, people began to spend large amounts of money on shopping that day. At first, Black Friday was an American event only. But now that more and more people shop online, shoppers in many countries take part in it. So why is it called Black Friday? The word "black" often has a bad meaning, especially when it is connected to a stock market crash. For example, Black Thursday, on October 24, 1929, was the start of the Great Depression. On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones fell by almost 22% in just one day. The "black" in Black Friday, however, means something different. Since stores offer huge discounts only on that day and so many people go shopping, it turned into the year's most profitable day for retailers. Accountants write profits in black and losses in red. That is why the day came to be called Black Friday: on this day, stores earn a lot of money and are "in the black." Today, there are other discount days, like Green Monday and Cyber Monday, yet Black Friday is still very important to retail businesses.
